meta.description: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence the poet said it. The line traces to broadcaster David Frost, earliest documented in a New Jersey newspaper in 1985.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't aim for success if you want it. Just do what you love and believe in, and it will come naturally'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the poet Robert Frost. Quote Investigator points to TV host David Frost, earliest documented 1985 — and the popular wording is a later variant.

answer.label: Not Robert Frost — most likely David Frost
answer.sourceLine: This is a surname collision. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence that the poet Robert Frost ever used the saying and calls the ascription to him probably spurious, pointing instead to the English television host Sir David Frost. The earliest citation anyone has produced is a celebrity-quotation quiz in the Courier-Post of Camden, New Jersey on 2 October 1985, whose answer key credited David Frost. No speech, book, interview or letter of Frost’s has been located as the original, so he is the likely — not the proven — author.
answer.confidenceText: Not the poet. The paper trail leads to a broadcaster, and even there it is secondhand.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “Out of the mouths of celebrities: Name the famous folks who’ve made some infamous statements” by Jerry Holderman
Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes: Wit and Wisdom for All Occasions (1997), p. 172
David Frost, the broadcaster — not Robert Frost, the poet

source.excerpt: I think success is a crappy, trendy word. Don’t aim for success if you want it. Just do what you love doing and it will come naturally.
trail: 2 October 1985 — the earliest citation on record. A celebrity-quotation quiz by Jerry Holderman in the Courier-Post of Camden, New Jersey credited the remark to the television host and journalist David Frost in its answer section, in the longer form beginning “I think success is a crappy, trendy word.” Quote Investigator transcribes the passage and cites page 11D, column 3 ↗.

23 January 1991 — the wording starts to shift. A profile of a local high-school student in The Record of Hackensack, New Jersey quoted the line as “just do what you love and believe in it, and it will come naturally,” with the student expressly attributing it to David Frost. QI cites the column and page 6 ↗.

1997 — the version you know gets fixed in print. Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes: Wit and Wisdom for All Occasions printed the sentence in essentially its modern form and credited DAVID FROST; QI verified the entry on paper at page 172. The book itself is catalogued by Open Library as a 1997 Reader’s Digest Association edition, Pleasantville, NY ↗.

By 2009 — the name changes. Quote Investigator records a tweet of 26 August 2009 carrying the saying under Robert Frost’s name; that is the earliest reassignment to the poet that QI documents, not necessarily the first that occurred. See QI’s chronology ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the fuller 1985 form as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the Courier-Post quiz, and the version QI recommends using. It differs from the sentence in circulation: 1985 has “what you love doing,” where the familiar version has “what you love and believe in.” Note also that the 1985 text is a newspaper columnist reporting the remark, not a transcript of Frost saying it.

source.rightsNote: Rights cannot be settled here, and it would be wrong to claim otherwise. This is certainly not public domain — every documented appearance of the sentence is modern, beginning with the Courier-Post of 2 October 1985 and running through Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes in 1997. But no rights holder can be named either, because the original utterance has never been located: the 1985 and 1991 texts are journalists reporting a remark rather than the work in which it first appeared, and Quote Investigator notes the earliest citations are indirect ↗. Quotle.info therefore asserts no copyright status for this line.

author.name: David Frost
author.heading: About David Frost
author.bio: Sir David Paradine Frost (7 April 1939 – 31 August 2013) was an English television host, journalist, comedian and writer. He is the ‘other Frost’ — a broadcaster rather than a poet — and his quotation footprint is a small fraction of Robert Frost’s, which is precisely the asymmetry that lets a line drift from him to the poet rather than the other way round. Even his own Wikiquote page carries only a handful of sourced lines and does not include this saying, so the credit to him rests on Quote Investigator’s newspaper trail rather than on anything Frost is documented as having published.

copyAttribution: "Don't aim for success if you want it; just do what you love and believe in, and it will come naturally." — usually credited to the poet Robert Frost, but Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence he said it and calls that ascription probably spurious. The likely originator is the English broadcaster Sir David Frost (1939–2013). The earliest documented citation is a Courier-Post (Camden, New Jersey) quiz of 2 October 1985, which credited David Frost; this wording is fixed in print in Reader's Digest Quotable Quotes (1997), p. 172, which reads "…if you want it: just do what you love and believe in…". No primary source from Frost himself has been located. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Two things are wrong with the version you saw
misattribution.intro: This quotation is misattributed and reworded. The name on it belongs to the wrong Frost, and the sentence itself is not the earliest recorded form.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states it found no substantive evidence that Robert Frost employed this saying, and that the ascription to him is probably spurious — the linkage arising from confusion with another person of the same surname. The earliest reassignment to the poet that QI documents is a tweet of 26 August 2009; every earlier citation names David Frost. Wikiquote’s Robert Frost page ↗ does not carry the line at all.

The sentence in circulation matches the entry in Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes (1997), not the earliest record. The 1985 Courier-Post text reads “just do what you love doing and it will come naturally,” preceded by “I think success is a crappy, trendy word” — a line the shareable version drops. QI recommends using the 1985 version ↗.
The error is live in both directions. TheQuotes.net lists the modern wording under Robert Frost ↗, while Goodreads credits David Frost ↗ — neither with a primary source.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: not Robert Frost. The saying most likely belongs to the broadcaster David Frost, but even that rests on secondhand newspaper reports beginning 2 October 1985 — as Quote Investigator sets out, calling him the most likely originator while noting the earliest citations are indirect ↗. No speech, book or interview of Frost’s has been produced as the source.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to the wrong Frost
lead: The sentence sounds like something a poet might say — unhurried, a little contrarian about ambition — and that is half of why it clings to Robert Frost. The other half is arithmetic: Robert Frost is one of the most quoted names on the internet, and David Frost is not. When a line is loose in circulation and two men share a surname, it flows toward the bigger name, never away from it. Quote Investigator ↗ puts the drift down to exactly that: confusion with another person whose last name was Frost.

The paper trail does not lead anywhere poetic. It leads to a newspaper puzzle. On 2 October 1985 the Courier-Post of Camden, New Jersey ran a quiz inviting readers to match famous statements to the people who made them; the answer key gave this one to the television host David Frost, in a longer and blunter form than the one that circulates today. Wikiquote, meanwhile, is no help in either direction — Robert Frost’s page ↗ has no Misattributed section and never carries the line, and David Frost’s ↗ does not contain it either.
context.detailsSummary: The wording changed on its way to you
detailsBody: The version you have almost certainly seen is not the earliest one. In the 1985 Courier-Post answer key the sentence reads “just do what you love doing and it will come naturally,” introduced by a line that no motivational poster ever reprints: “I think success is a crappy, trendy word.”

The familiar “love and believe in” phrasing shows up later. A 1991 profile in The Record of Hackensack, New Jersey has a student quoting David Frost with “what you love and believe in it”; the 1997 collection Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes prints it without that stray “it,” and that is the wording in circulation now. Quote Investigator recommends using the 1985 form ↗, because the later ones are further from the earliest record.
So the popular sentence is doubly displaced: the wrong Frost, and a wording that arrived a dozen years after the earliest citation rather than from the speaker’s mouth.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator states it has found no substantive evidence that Robert Frost employed this saying; that the linkage was probably caused by confusion with another person whose last name was Frost; that David Frost is the most likely originator and the Robert Frost ascription is probably spurious; that the precise phrasing is uncertain because the earliest citations are indirect; and that QI suggests using the 1985 version. It documents the 1985-10-02 Courier-Post (Camden, NJ) quiz by Jerry Holderman, p. 11D col. 3, reading 'I think success is a crappy, trendy word. Don't aim for success if you want it. Just do what you love doing and it will come naturally'; the 1991-01-23 Record (Hackensack, NJ) profile by Pearl J. Park, p. 6; the 1997 Reader's Digest Quotable Quotes, p. 172 col. 2, Pleasantville NY; and an August 26, 2009 tweet reassigning it to Robert Frost.
Quote Investigator's David Frost tag page indexes the article investigating this quotation.

Wikiquote's Robert Frost page has only the top-level sections Quotes, Quotes about Robert Frost and External links — no Misattributed or Disputed section — and the phrase 'aim for success' does not appear anywhere on the page.

Wikiquote's David Frost page does not contain this saying; its sourced quotations are the catchphrases 'Hello, good evening and welcome' and 'Seriously, though, he's doing a grand job!', plus a line from The Independent (16 September 1989), with no Sourced/Unsourced section split.

Open Library catalogues 'Reader's Digest Quotable Quotes', by the Reader's Digest Association, first published 1997, in a 1997 edition subtitled 'wit and wisdom for all occasions from America's most popular magazine', ISBN 0895779250, 216 pages, published in Pleasantville, N.Y.
Wikipedia's opening sentence reads: 'Sir David Paradine Frost (7 April 1939 – 31 August 2013) was an English television host, journalist, comedian, and writer.'
Wikipedia's opening sentence reads: 'Robert Lee Frost (March 26, 1874 – January 29, 1963) was an American poet.'

TheQuotes.net lists 'Don't aim for success if you want it; just do what you love and believe in, and it will come naturally.' on a page of Robert Frost quotes — i.e. the misattribution is still live with the modern wording.
Goodreads presents 'Don't aim for success if you want it; just do what you love and believe in, and it will come naturally.' attributed to David Frost.
